utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kotur.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. Hannis will now continue. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. I wanted to resume. I got side-tracked but I wanted to finish talking about the Reka action, and I'd like to show you Exhibit P2026. And, Colonel, I'll tell you this is from the 125th Motorised Brigade. It's a regular combat report. It's dated the 29th of April. And if you could go to item number 2 for me, and in the second paragraph, the second sentence in my English translation says: "Operation or action Reka was completed on 28 April." Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You mean item 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, under item number 2 and then it's the second paragraph. Could you read for us what follows there after the reference to completion of the Reka action?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The remaining units of the brigade continue with fortifying setting up obstacles, making mock combat positions, clearing the roads and the front line. On 28th of April, Operation Reka was completed. The 1st Company of the 1st Battalion and the volunteer company were those of our units that were involved. A volunteer was slightly wounded. The operation was both successful and completed."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "During --"

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When we spoke yesterday, I believe you had indicated to us that your recollection was that the units that were participating in the -- assisting the MUP in mopping up that an area were elements of the 63rd Parachute Brigade and 52nd Military Police Battalion. Do you recall telling us that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were -- and we have had evidence in this case, at least about the 63rd Parachute Brigade. So does this refresh your memory as to additional elements of the VJ that were engaged in the Reka action?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see here are units of the 125th Motorised Brigade. These units were doing no more than protecting their own combat disposition and their own elements of combat disposition. As far as I know, they were sometime between Smonica to the south towards Junik and somewhere around Dobros, but as far as I know, these units were certainly not involved in searching and clearing the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You will see in the next paragraph the statement that says: "The commander and the chief of staff of the Pristina Corps were in the brigade from 0900 to 1200 hours today," which was the 29th of April.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm having trouble hearing the interpretation. I'm straining to actually listen to it. Now it's a little better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Should I repeat the question for you then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see the next paragraph says that: "The commander and the chief of staff of the Pristina Corps were in the brigade from 0900 to 1200 hours today." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the last paragraph before item 3. That's what you mean. The brigade command team. Is that the one you're referring to or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. My translation says "The commander and the chief of staff." And that would be General Lazarevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just tell me the paragraph? I'm looking for it and I can't seem to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- The one you were reading. Could you just go one sentence earlier and read that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] It's been indicated to me. I see it now. From 0900 to 1200 hours today the commander and chief of staff of the Pristina Corps were in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall General Lazarevic during the 125th on the 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard something like that but I wasn't there. And I'm not privy to any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where were you, Colonel, on the 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the units of the 125th Motorised Brigade. We were either in the 3rd Battalion, the 2nd, or one of the other units. That's where we were spending all of our time. You have reports to show that. There were reports sent by the forward command post command to the Pristina Corps command. They say that we were providing assistance each day to the 125th Motorised Brigade with the objective of consolidating our defence lines. This was an ongoing task, all the way up until the brigade withdrew --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from Kosovo and Metohija altogether. You will find that in all of the daily reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes but you understand, Colonel, that doesn't give me enough detail to know whether or not the fact that you're with the 125th Brigade on the 29th of April and General Lazarevic is shown as being in the 125th Brigade on the 29th. I don't know whether you two saw each other on that day. Can you tell me specifically where you were on the 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly didn't see each other. I don't remember that. I don't remember us meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You told us yesterday at page 40, line 1, you were asked by Mr. Bakrac whether General Lazarevic was in Djakovica on the 27th or 28th of April, and your answer was, no, he was not in Djakovica. You were then asked had he been in Djakovica would you have known, and your answer was, "Yes, I would have known that, certainly." How was it you would have known where General Lazarevic was on the 27th and 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I would have known whether General Lazarevic had been in Djakovica or not on the 27th and 28th. I meant the forward command post, whether he was there, not in the 125th or 549th or 252nd Armoured Brigade. That's not what I had in mind. There were a great many units across Kosovo-Metohija and near Djakovica, but when I said I would have known that he'd been in Djakovica, I meant the forward command post, which is where we were staying at the time, because the operations officer would have written that down. We would have certainly know when a commander was around or something like that. If I had not been there at the time perhaps I would have been notified in the course of the day as for any other units, I really don't know: When he was there, where he was, and whether he was anywhere. Maybe on the 29th he was in the 125th, but I certainly didn't meet him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you probably have to slow down a bit again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was going to say, Mr. Hannis, before we get into the warnings from the interpreters, Mr. Kotur, please remember what happened yesterday and do your best to slow down. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is it correct, Colonel, that the -- the war diary of the forward command post and/or the war diary of the Pristina Corps command in April 1999 would reflect where the commander was on any particular day? Is that information that normally would have been entered into the war diary?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that sort of information should have been entered into the war log if the commander was away from the command post during the day. That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Have you seen the -- the war diary or the war log for the forward command post of the Pristina Corps or for the Pristina Corps command since the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just tell you one thing. The forward command post is not the one keeping the war log. They will are under no obligation to keep a war log. The war log is only keep at the Pristina Corps command. At its forward command post this document is just not kept. After the war I didn't see the war log of the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you ever heard anything about where it went, because we have not been able to find it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a year I left the Pristina Corps and I left for the Novi Sad Corps, and I know nothing about their documents, about the situation in the Pristina Corps or anything else for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could we look at a map now, Exhibit P615, at page 22 in e-court. Colonel, you mentioned a location called Osek Hilja. I hope I'm pronouncing that approximately right. And if we could enlarge the upper left two quadrants. I hope that will show what I want the colonel to look at. Maybe one more time. Thank you. Colonel, can you see that map on your monitor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see on the road leading sort of north, north-west out of Djakovica what appears to be that -- that name or that village, Osek Hilja. Is that the one you were telling us about yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that looks like that's just a kilometre or so outside of Djakovica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. I see Osek Pasa but I don't see Osek Hilja. A while ago when I said that I saw it, I was wrong. It says Osek Pasa, and Osek Hilja, I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you move directly to the left of Osek Pasa and tell us if you don't see Osek Hilja there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do now. Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Unfortunately this is right on the page dividing line in our map, but do you recall approximately what distance is that from Djakovica? It looks very -- very near.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably over a kilometre. I don't know what the scale is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to page 21 of this exhibit. Colonel, I'm going to show you the course -- the next page adjacent to this one where Osek Hilja is also shown, but you can't see Djakovica on this other page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could zoom in on the upper right two quadrants. Yes. And scroll down just a little bit for me, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, are you able to see Osek Hilja on this map? It's near the right edge, about two-thirds of the way down. Do you find it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you told us yesterday that from Osek Hilja you could see part of the -- the Reka area or the -- the Caragoj Valley; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that from Osek Hilja you could see part of the Reka area, I didn't mean from the village itself, the village of Osek Hilja. I meant the Cabrat ridge above the village itself. If you go there, you can actually see it. From the village itself, you can see nothing at all. There's a road there you take through Osek Hilja and it leads up to the Cabrat ridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you left Osek Hilja on that day where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went up to the Cabrat ridge above Osek Hilja.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were asked in connection with around this time of the 27th and 28th of April about what Nike Peraj had said. Mr. Peraj had said that General Lazarevic spent most of his time in Djakovica, and at page 44, line 5, you said -- this is what it says in the transcript, and maybe you can help -- help me with this. You're quoting as saying: "General Lazarevic was in Djakovica on the 10th or -- or, rather, he -- when he was in the 122nd Motorised Brigade because of Kosare, I think he maybe just passed through once or twice but that's all. He did not, definitely did not, spend most of his time in Djakovica." Now, I think -- I think there's an error there. It wouldn't be the 122nd Motorised Brigade. You would have been referring to the 125th; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no 122nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And so you must have been referring to the 125th; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what about this part where it says: "Lazarevic was in Djakovica on the 10th"? Do you know what you're referring to there? You're talking about the 10th of April or 10th of May, 10th of March?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you looked at my statement, if you looked through my statement all the way to the end, I believe that I said that on the 10th of April I'd been called to the command post of the Pristina Corps through the command of the 243rd Mechanised Brigade. I didn't know the reason for that until I got to the command post. When I came there, I found General Pavkovic, who told me that General Lazarevic was in Djakovica, or more precisely at Kosare because of the fall of Kosare rather because of the incursion of terrorist forces from Albanian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We do have that. You told us before. I was just trying to clear up that this 10th meant the 10th of April. And you say maybe he passed through once or twice. Do you know if he passed through sometime around the 29th of April when he was in the 125th Brigade as reflected in this combat report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether he passed through Djakovica on the 29th. I don't know which road he took to get there. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have taken the only road that was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned that Nike Peraj had -- well, we talked about the evidence about Nike Peraj receiving permission to visit his village. To your knowledge was the -- was the combat action in that area completed so that it would have been safe for Captain Peraj to travel to his home in that area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which date you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the 28th of April, up until the end of that day or by the end of that day the operation had been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was planned, to go on for two days, the 27th and the 28th. It was completed that -- sometime like 1700, 1800, 1900 hours that afternoon. I'm not sure when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I want to turn to another topic now, and first I want to direct your attention to your testimony in Milosevic at page 47487. And this has to do with the KVM mission and verification, and in answer to a question from Mr. Nice, you said at line 24: "Not a single unit was brought to Kosovo without notification to the KVM. There was not a single movement, not a single entry or exit from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Nothing was done without notifying the KVM." Is that still your position today?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you were aware of elements of the 37th Motorised Brigade from the 2nd Army being brought into Kosovo in early March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a combat group belonging to the 37th Motorised Brigade was brought to Kosovo and Metohija in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the KVM was not notified about that, were they?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When and how?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each day we exchanged information about the movements of vehicles in Kosovo and Metohija in case there were more than five vehicles moving about regardless of whether the unit in question was moving just in the Kosovo area, whether it left Kosovo or whether it entered Kosovo and Metohija. Suppose there was a single unit entering, a somewhat larger unit, more than five vehicles. We knew immediately that members of the verification mission would notice --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would just like to know when did you notify the KVM about the 37th Motorised Brigade coming into Kosovo, and how did you do that? Who did you tell?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain right now whether I was the one who did that or whether it was the new team that started working as of the 10th of March. I can't remember the exact date when the combat group arrived in Kosovo and Metohija. In principle they arrived in March. I know that much. I was there up until the 10th of March. I was in charge of those meetings. But after that date I was no longer the one who chaired those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we -- we have evidence I could show you from the 37th itself indicating they came to Kosovo Mitrovica on the 7th of March, 1999. Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they arrived on the 7th of March then Ciaglinski knew it, and I knew it; and I'm sure he was told at one of the meetings he had with me, or someone from my team would have told him anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness answered, but I wish to raise a matter of principle here. If Mr. Hannis wants to show the witness a document, let him tell us which document it is to see if he knows that particular document, and the witness can see but all right the witness provided an answer before Mr. Hannis gave us the number, so fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, I would indicate Exhibit P2039, the daily combat report from the 37th Brigade as my source for that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I would direct your attention then to your testimony in Milosevic at page 47534, and you were being asked about a notebook that apparently you had with you when you testified in Milosevic. Do you recall that -- do you recall that notebook?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you read some of the entries in that notebook, and do you recall that the last entry in that notebook as you testified at page 47535, was on the 9th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the last date I entered something into that notebook was the 9th of March. As of that date onwards, there are no further entries in that notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at page 47535, you read one of the entries from -- I believe it's the 9th of March that said: "37th group brought in." So according to that it appears on the 9th of March you had an entry in your notebook that the 37th had come in, and I assume that means come into Kosovo; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And that 37th Motorised Brigade was -- was a VJ unit that was outside barracks, and that was not one of the three groups that was permitted under the agreement, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we interpreted the agreement, it allowed us, if we assessed our security to be under threat, to take everything in our power, all measures in our power, to defend ourselves and to reduce the threat to the greatest possible extent. In March, in view of the assessments we had carried out, we were already taking measures against the expected aggression, and one such measure was what you saw in the notebook, that is, bringing in this unit to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. This unit arrived pursuant to an order from the Chief of the General Staff or some other army commander. They certainly did not come on their own initiative. According to the agreement, we had a right to this. That's why I said we never broke the agreement or violated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I think you're overstating it, Colonel, if you say you never violated the agreement. Let me show you Exhibit 3D484. This is -- these are the minutes of the VJ collegium from the 10th of December, 1998, and maybe it will make it easier if I hand you a hard copy, because it's several pages. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a moment, please. I'm checking, but it seems that this document was not announced. I do apologise to my learned friend if that is not the case, but it seems to be unannounced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's on my list. My case manager is checking for me. I'm told I have 584 and not 384, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So, Colonel, is it your position --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 486 in the transcript. What document is this? What's the number of the document? In the transcript it's 484.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I have, 484. And I think what is on my list as 584.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis is claiming it's a typographical error. Do you oppose this?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do because this is the second document already. Yesterday, we had another document that was not announced but was used. Now we have this document, and in that case we won't need the lists any longer unless we follow instructions and announce the precise documents to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm okay to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Carry on, Mr. Hannis, as you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel, we'll skip that one. I'll show you a different one, and when I get the hard copy I'll trade with you. Let me go to another VJ collegium minute, and I'll hand you the hand copy of this one. This is from the 25th of February, 1999, and this is Exhibit Number P941. Colonel, if you could in your hard copy go to page -- I think it's page number 15, and in e-court the B/C/S is page number 16 because the cover page doesn't have a number. Actually, if you'll look at page 14. If we could go back one page. In the e-court to page 15 in B/C/S, and it's page 15 in English. Let me start with the part that says "Conclusion." Do you find that? It's right above where there's a reference to General Ojdanic speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may assist. Both pages are in English, but now we do have the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I will tell you this is General Curcin speaking, and in conclusion he says: "The week behind us was characterised by the upgrading the 3rd Army and part of the VJ units planned to be used in Kosovo and Metohija to full combat readiness." Then we go to Colonel Dimitrijevic who says: "With respect to the departure of an anti-terrorist battalion from the 72nd Special Brigade for Kosovo and Metohija, I found it inappropriate that nobody had ever consulted me about it." Were you aware that prior to the 25th February, 1999, elements of the 72nd Special Brigade had come into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I knew this, but I know that part of this unit, and it says so here, was in part of Kacanik fighting against the terrorist units closing off that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The thing I want to know is did you know that they'd gone in Kosovo? You didn't, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So as far as you know, it was not reported to KVM, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was not reported by me. Perhaps something was done at the level of the General Staff with their team. Maybe it was done at that level. It's possible, but I was not informed. Although I don't really recall this detail. To be more precise, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you'll go to the next page in the B/C/S. General Curcin is speaking, and he says at the proposal of the 3rd Army command and after the assistant Chief for Operations, the staff sector of the chief of General Staff made a decision and issued an order which was implemented. And then he goes on and says you're ordered, General, not to split the units that are being sent down there but to use them as a whole has not been obeyed. Ojdanic says and not to bring them to Kosovo. That's the essence of the matter. Would you agree with me from what we've just looked at that even General Dimitrijevic and General Ojdanic may not have been fully informed about the 72nd Special Brigade being brought into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I'm not aware of what relations there were between them, why Dimitrijevic would speak in at that way or somebody else. All I know in general is that we had a legitimate right, in view of the forthcoming aggression to prepare our defence against the aggression to the best of our ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not the point, and that's not my question. The question has to do with whether or not you were informed and whether or not the KVM was being informed as they were supposed to be under the agreement; and you didn't know about it. Is looks like some of the guys on the General Staff didn't know about it. So how can -- how can the KVM be informed under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend is providing an answer and making the witness speculate. The witness has said that he didn't know whether the team at the level of the General Staff had informed the mission or not. He said that quite clearly. Now my learned friend is making him speculate and putting a different response into his mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honour, very briefly? Whenever Mr. Hannis puts a question he speaks as if the entire 72nd Brigade went there or the other -- entire. He always refers to entire brigades, and it was only parts of brigades. I would like that to be made clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Hannis, you're essentially asking the witness questions that are for us to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, before we leave this document could you go to page 18 in your hard copy. This is page 19 in the e-court. And if you find -- it's page 19 of the English in e-court as well. If you could find where General Obradovic is speaking. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the second paragraph under his remarks says in my translation: "Secondly, I support the idea that we must not send even the smallest number of troops to Kosovo because I'm afraid it might be purposely construed as a breach of certain provisions in the agreement and because a minor issue can become a very complicated one. Therefore, I would suggest that not even the smallest of units be sent to Kosovo and Metohija in the next ten days because we are bound by the current agreement to inform them of everything going into or out of Kosovo, et cetera." And that's consistent with your understanding, isn't it, that you were bound to inform KVM about all of the troop movements in and out of Kosovo; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our obligation to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you just give me a moment, Colonel. Related to this early in your testimony on Friday last week, you were shown an exhibit by Mr. Bakrac which had a schematic map of Kosovo diagramming various groups that the OSCE observed to be out of barracks in their view; and in your answer one thing you talked about was at page 108 on Friday, page 108, line 7, under the agreement the Pristina Corps was allowed to have three groups across the area, and these groups were in Stimlje, in Dulje. That was one group in two different locations. The other group was in Volujak area, and the third group was in the Lapusnik area, or, rather, the rear of that group was in Komorane. It was also one in the same group in two different locations. Let me stop you there and ask you this: So as I understand that, you say these three groups were in five locations; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Colonel Ciaglinski told us that in his conversations with members of the commission on cooperation, I don't remember now if he said he heard it from you or from Loncar that the VJ took the view that the entirety of the province of Kosovo was considered by the VJ to be a training ground. Are you aware that Colonel Ciaglinski testified to that or that's in his statement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What Ciaglinski said is a total falsehood.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So it's not your view that the entirety of Kosovo is a training ground?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not just my view. It's the truth. Mr. Ciaglinski received a map with all the training grounds entered in where the Pristina Corps was conducting training for the military on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. These were permanent shooting ranges and training grounds. And he received that map. That's why I'm saying that Mr. Ciaglinski is not telling the truth. It was not all of Kosovo, not the entire territory, only those places that had been designated for the purpose for decades.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, one of the things that I -- I'm sorry, did you want to say --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say for years. I may have been exaggerated when I said for decades. I didn't use the most precise term.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In -- in one of your answers earlier when you were talking about alleged incidents with the KVM, I think you described for us there were occasions where the KVM was driving down a road and they came to a village where elements of the VJ were deployed, and then they had to either stop and call and get permission or they had to go around. Is that accurate? Do you recall incidents like that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- and we've heard other evidence that I think indicated that it appears that the VJ considered some inhabited areas, villages, to be within their training area. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you aware of an incident in Podujevo in late December 1998 where VJ elements were purportedly engaged in an exercise and then were fired upon and responded, and there was some -- some controversy about that with the -- with the OSCE mission? Did you know about that incident?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to see the document mentioning this to jog my memory. After a lapse of ten years, it's difficult to recall the specific events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fair. Let me -- let me read you something and I'll ask you if this refreshes your memory or if you heard anything about this. This is from a VJ collegium session on the 30th of December, 1998, and it's General Dimitrijevic speaking. It's Exhibit number P928 [Realtime transcript read in error "P9208"]. I'll just read it to you now to try and save a little time. He says: "In addition, the current situation in the vicinity of Podujevo, I think we must be completely consistent here and completely open towards each other, so to speak. This situation in Podujevo and the surroundings, it was complex before, but when did it suddenly become even more complicated? After the so-called pretend or real planned exercises in which this company took part in the field, General, these sorts of moves will lead us to disaster. The explanation that this was a planned exercise, that is not true. It was planned that the unit would provoke the terrorists so that the MUP would then have to do whatever it had to do." Hearing that, does that refresh your memory about an incident in Podujevo in late December 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listening to this I realised that General Dimitrijevic had no idea what the situation in Podujevo was. If Ciaglinski made a statement, I think he could have said -- well, he told me there were 3.000 terrorists there already. They were digging trenches along the roads. Before the verification mission arrived, they hadn't been there at all, and we hadn't had any problems as regards the passability of roads. The road from Nis via Podujevo to Pristina. We didn't have any problems there until December. This statement by Dimitrijevic really surprises me, that he said that at the collegium. I find that really surprising. I think it's nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You know what General Dimitrijevic's position was in the army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know very well what his position was, and I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you saying that he was not well-informed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either he was not well-informed or he said those things intentionally. Those are the only two options I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't allow for the possibility that he was well-informed and he was correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was not correct. I think Ciaglinski said he even got a medal because of the situation in Podujevo when he went to Britain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, what do you mean by either he was well-informed -- sorry, either he was not well-informed or he was saying these things intentionally? What do you mean by the second of these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant to say by this was that Dimitrijevic was opposed to the command. I knew that, and that's why I said what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis the number for this exhibit is it P928?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I'll check, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's just been recorded as 9208.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It should be 928, 928.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, when you say Dimitrijevic was opposed to the command, what exactly do you mean? Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that, I meant to say that the security service was beyond the command. It was -- it didn't want to obey the command, and Dimitrijevic was at the head of that service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what's the source of your information for that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal experience with his service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the nature of your personal experience? Did you have personal dealings with him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with his organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, did you have personal experience with General Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw him once, but I had experience with his organs and assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there anything about your one personal experience with General Dimitrijevic that would support your view that he was opposed to the command? I'm just talking about that one personal experience with him.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm about to tell you something but I'm not sure that will be sufficient for you to fathom the situation, and you might -- you might not find my answer satisfactory, but I'm going to tell you this: At the corps command level and at the brigade command level, if one discusses something, maybe a person to be sent for further training or education, maybe an appointment, anything at all, and a commander considers this as something that should be done, and then one of the security organs takes the floor and says, "Well, you know, we have something there, so don't." That's as good as a done thing. No explanation. No further information provided or anything like that. What is most frequently the case is that there is no negative work or poor situation with those people behind it, rather some sort of a clash of personalities. And this would be most efficiently dealt with through the security service, with their officers. I mean, I don't want to go into any details. That is of no relevance for this trial. This is my position, my opinion. That's all I'm saying. I have a firm position on these issues, and that's what I believe them to be like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you a question about the 37th Brigade that came in -- parts of it came in and, I believe, the 7th of March, 1999. Is it your position that they came in to defend the territory, or were they coming in to engage in training?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 37th was not there for training. It was there to fight the terrorist forces, the terrorist forces that by that time had already significantly gained in strength in Kosovo and Metohija. They were also there to perform day-to-day activities. They jeopardised the entire territory and any movements throughout the territory. Something similar to what actually was the case in June and July 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we have a look at Exhibit P2039. Colonel, this is a daily operational report from the 37th Motorised Brigade, dated the 20th of March. I -- oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem seems to be resolved. Can you -- no. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's not about the document. I think my learned friend has exceeded his time. I stood up before the document was brought up, but then he started asking the question. I just sat down, but now that my learned friend Mr. Hannis has stopped, I think that I am allocated for my re-examination and the examination granted to Mr. Ivetic has already been exceeded by at least half an hour according to my calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have the math in front of me, but that sounds about right. I think I have another 15 minutes I would like to -- to go. I have this document and then some matters related to Ciaglinski and credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The situation here is are fairly exceptional, Mr. Bakrac. We have a fairly lengthy transcript, as you know, initially tendered as the evidence of this witness and departed from and then a number of obvious lines to be followed in cross-examination based on the extent of the information available to the Prosecution. Mr. Hannis again is being fairly focused in his cross-examination. There have been occasions when the Prosecution have not exceeded the time, in fact have been significantly under the time that could have been used if you take it on an individual witness basis; and as you know, we've always viewed the time in the end of the day as global and have been prepared to extend the time available in individual cases if it's not going to exceed the global figure and it can be justified in the individual case, and here that does appear to us to be the situation. And bearing in mind that there are only two issues to be pursued, we shall allow Mr. Hannis that extra 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, as I said, this is 20 March 1999, the daily operational report from the 37th. You'll see under 5.3 it says: "On 7 March 1999, the 37th mtbr stand-by forces departed to the general area of Kosovska Mitrovica with the aim of carrying out exercises ..." I will tell you also that in this case at transcript page 19926, line 23, Colonel Djikovic [sic] himself, or General Dikovic now told us that they were coming for training. Are you willing to agree that your previous answer about that is mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe what General Zivanovic said they were there for training and that's true. Our units don't have professional soldiers. They're not well-trained soldiers. In the Kosovska Mitrovica area or sector, there is Zimusa [phoen], which is a training ground, and I'm sure that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've answered my questions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- these units were trained there and prepared for combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you know there's in the evidence in this case and -- well, in the Milosevic case there was a dispute between the evidence of Colonel Ciaglinski and your evidence about certain events. You know about that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. Just a minute, please, before we go too far. By that time it will be too late. Mr. Hannis talked about Djikovic. That's what the transcript reflects, and in my earphones I heard Zivkovic, and then the witness said Zivanovic. Can we please ascertain who this person was, because I think the interpretation was wrong. It was Zivkovic instead of Djikovic. I think my learned friend Mr. Hannis had Dikovic in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure of my pronunciation but I'm referring to the one who is the commander of the 37th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we all know that but can you help us further with the name? I remember the evidence, but I don't remember who gave it by name. Are you satisfied with that explanation, Mr. Bakrac, that it's the commander of the group of the 37th that came to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour. Dikovic. It's just that the witness was told through his headset that it was Zivkovic, and then he said Zivanovic as commander, and he doesn't know who said what, so I thought that might lead to some confusion in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this -- this dispute in the evidence actually started when Colonel Ciaglinski testified in closed session in Milosevic case, and part of his evidence was that he had met with you on a particular occasion and you had given him a map and purportedly told him about a plan to expel the KLA and the civilian Albanian population from Kosovo; right? That's the gist of how this whole thing started; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski, there was this closed session that was open but it was closed when Ciaglinski testified. He said that I disclosed to him a plan to expel the Siptar population from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this. It's my understanding from his testimony and your testimony that during the time that you worked together in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999 it seems that you -- you each respected the other and viewed the other as professional and honest in your work. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that I was acting in a professional, responsible, and conscientious manner, and I thought that Ciaglinski was doing the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the statements that he made to me at various meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you told us in the Milosevic case at page 47469 that you became aware of this closed-session testimony "in Belgrade from my colleagues," and you were asked which colleagues. You said: "The colleagues who worked with me." Mr. Nice asked you for names and then you said you couldn't say. And then you said: "And I really am not going to name any names, because I'm not quite sure who said it. So I really -- I don't really want to give anybody any trouble." We can go into closed session right now, Colonel, if that would help, but I would like to know the names of the colleague or colleagues who told you about what Ciaglinski had said in closed session. If we go into closed session will you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No need for closed session. I simply don't know what to say. I don't know who it was. That said it. I can't remember. There were a number of people, and I don't want to name a single name, which perhaps would not be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, just before you proceed further, I take it what was heard in closed session before is now public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't need to be concerned about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, we don't. It became public in Milosevic, and then it's been public in our earlier proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me it's likely to be a fairly small number of individuals who could have told you about that. How many -- how many are you talking about? Is it one of six or one of ten?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might as well say 50. There were four or five of us in that office when I was told. I don't know who it was that said it. Therefore, I will not go any further. They were all people in positions of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you understand if we knew the names of one of those four or five that might help us follow up on how that information came to you. Can you name in closed session for us any of those four or five persons, or is it simply that you refuse to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really don't see that this is something that is at stake in this trial. I really don't see the need to further investigate this, whether some information was shared from the Milosevic case and waste time like this and use this witness for this purpose. I think the Prosecutor is free to perhaps call this witness at a later date and investigate the matter. I just don't see how it's relevant to our trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I disagree entirely, Mr. Bakrac. This is an extremely relevant issues because the credibility of both this witness and Ciaglinski, who are two very important witnesses, is at stake, and the question's a very simple one, and the witness clearly can give more information than he is giving without necessarily committing himself to the identity of the person from whom he got the particular piece of information that mattered. So the inquiry being conducted by Mr. Hannis is a legitimate exercise of his cross-examination time. So please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, can you name any of those four or five persons? And if you like, we can go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You can't or you won't?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Because you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. Not by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This was a fairly significant and probably startling event for you, was it not, to be told that Ciaglinski had testified in the Milosevic trial and said you gave him a map and told him about VJ plans, and you're hearing this from your VJ colleagues. That must have been a pretty exciting event. Wasn't it? Just yes or no for now.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exciting because it's not true. That's one thing. And the other is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Untrue events can be just as exciting or more exciting than true ones, can't they? We get angry and we get outraged when somebody says something untrue about us; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, sir, I saw on TV when Ciaglinski testified in open session at least. What he said in open session, when he used a felt pen to draw a plan on a map. It was all perfectly clear to officers at the corps command who knew me, immediately it was clear to them that Ciaglinski had me in mind. That's what he said in open session. He nearly drew my picture without saying the name. Why? Every day I had a meeting with him at 10.00. It was a compulsory meeting. There were many such meetings. And I -- in closed session he drops the name. I didn't know some of the things that he said in open session that I was a patriot, a Serb, military officer, and everything else that he said about me, my authority that even the higher ranking officers were afraid of me and all those impressions that he shared I heard that when I came here; but about the expulsion plan, this is something that he drew on the map and that's what matter to you. And we all knew that, and what did it matter if somebody said well, Kotur, that's you. Well we all knew that so I don't think I was particularly excited, so that much is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, your wife at some point in time was excited about it, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: She called Colonel Ciaglinski and told him that he had ruined your lives. You knew Ciaglinski testified about that. Is it -- is it correct that she called him? Just, first of all, did she call him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: She called him because I wanted her to, and she did. She didn't call without me knowing about it, but I explained why we had called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And, yeah, I want to ask you about that. He testified, I think, in April 2002, and his testimony here in this trial was that he got the call from your wife about a year after that. Do you recall when she made the phone call, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I know it was over a year after that. I had left the Pristina Corps by this time and was now at Novi Sad. Maybe he has a call identification number, and if he does he could tell that it was from Novi Sad and not from Nis or from Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, his evidence is it was about a year later so we'll say sometime in 2003, and your evidence in Milosevic was that she called him because she wanted to check on your apartment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which -- which apartment was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife's apartment at Belgrade Street 52. The same street where the verification mission was stationed, and that's where Mr. Drewienkiewicz lived. The flat was never returned to me. Right now there is Agim Ceku's brother staying there. We sued them, and although we won the case we still haven't managed to have our flat returned to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So -- in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So 2003, almost four years after you had left Kosovo, your wife suddenly out of the blue calls Ciaglinski to ask about your apartment. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying. I'm telling you this: I was renting at the time. I had nowhere to live, no flat of my own, because my flat had been taken by someone else. I was thinking maybe about the possibility of renting this flat to one of the people down there from the verification mission. I knew that Ciaglinski had been training this unit in Germany, and I know that he came with Jackson, he and Mr. Drewienkiewicz were the first to enter Kosovo and Metohija on day one, and he told me he knew many officers from that unit. It was only logical, since I was in trouble, and I still don't own a flat, that I should go and speak to someone who I believe could be of some assistance, and that was the reason. And I said that Ciaglinski called us, and he informed us, and you talk to him you've probably heard that, too, that a young married couple from Pec were now living in that flat. And I think my wife wished him a merry Christmas and that was the extent of Ciaglinski's conversation with my wife. I never called him because I don't speak English. My wife speaks perfect English and that's why she was the one to call because she was the better person to speak to him since I wasn't able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, you gave Mr. Ciaglinski a map during that meeting, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The meeting Ciaglinski testified about receiving a map from you and being told about the plan.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ciaglinski, I didn't -- Ciaglinski, all he got from us was a blank map at his own request, no plan to speak of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ciaglinski has two statements about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you give him a map?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He got a blank map, 1:100.000 Kosovo and Metohija. That was the scale, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I suggest what really happened is that you and Ciaglinski worked together. You got along well. You respected even other professionally and you may have gone maybe little bit further than you should have. You gave him that map and you told him a little bit about what the plan was. When he testified, and that came to light, you found yourself between a rock and a very hard place; and you had to deny Ciaglinski's evidence and your story about why your wife called him doesn't make sense. Isn't that the truth? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish you could call Ciaglinski again. I don't think he could possibly confirm what you just said. He would confirm my story as to why my wife had called him. That's what the conversation was about. It was in passing that she asked him why he had said that. He said he had just praised me and saying things that had nothing to do with anything at all. And then I heard later what I heard and saw the transcript from here so there. You know one thing -- what I want to know is did Ciaglinski ever say that to any of his superior officers?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you just trying to tell me no in a long way?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll take that as a no and stop now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, there's a number of references been made to the Milosevic transcript. How are we going to deal with these?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has an exhibit number, a 5D exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But only a small part of it has been referred to in the course of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in your hands. If you'd like us to prepare extracts regarding the sections that I've referred to and submit that as a separate exhibit number I'd be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As far as I can tell the parts referred to are 47482 and 83, 518, 523 and 24 and 25, 47487, 47534 and 35, and then passages in relation to the exchange over the map and over the telephone call which have not been specified in the course of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would indicate those are 47469 through 473. And then briefly again at 47530, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will consider how that should be dealt with during the break. We will have our break now, I think. Mr. Kotur, we have to break for 20 minutes at this stage. Could you again leave the courtroom with the usher. We'll resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, if these various pages are admitted, are there other parts of the transcript which you would seek to have admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. That was why I wanted live testimony. There's nothing else we wish to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you should compile a filing which extracts the parts which you have referred to, including the larger section you've just referred to towards the end and submit that and these parts will be admitted in the absence of any objection being stated to them within the seven days of the filing being filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll do that, Your Honour. Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mentioned, Mr. Kotur, that you wish that Mr. Ciaglinski had been asked again about the conversation with your wife. He was, of course, asked here in this trial about communication with your wife, and he referred to two communications that there were, one about the flat but one quite separately about the events that Mr. Hannis was raising with you. Were you aware that she had contacted Ciaglinski on two occasions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, and I said so at Mr. Milosevic's trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The circumstances in which you came to learn of the account Ciaglinski gave in the Milosevic trial about the map are not entirely clear to me. You say that the fact that you had been mentioned specifically in that context in the trial was drawn to your attention by a colleague. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You do not know wish colleague now, you can't remember, but am I also right in understanding you to say that it was one of a number of people who were together at the time it was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, if I understood the question correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what Mr. Hannis was asking you was simply to give us the names of even one of these, and that would enable him to carry out inquiries which may indeed confirm what you're saying. Now, why won't you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bonomy, anyone who followed the trial on television and it was broadcast every day in our part of the world when the Milosevic trial was on, what Mr. Ciaglinski said, well, everybody knew he was talking about me. So did I. When he drew the map and so on, everybody could tell who he was referring to because there was nobody else he had contacts with on behalf of the army of Yugoslavia. It was neither the Judge nor anyone from the Tribunal or any of Milosevic's advisors who told me this. It was my colleagues who said to me, "It was you. You are the one he was talking about." And I said, "Well, yes. Yes, I was." Everybody could tell. My colleagues could tell when they saw the Milosevic trial. That's the problem, not something else. There were five or six of us in the office. I can't recall which of us precisely said, "It was you he was talking about." That's the gist of it. It's not that I'm trying to conceal anything. Everything was clear. He didn't mention my name, but it was all clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that an explanation you gave in the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not in such detail, but I did say that it was quite clear he was referring to me and that everybody could guess that, and that's what I said in the Milosevic trial. What Ciaglinski said at the trial, everybody could tell it was about me, people from my team, from the corps command, all the colleagues who knew me. They all knew I had cooperated with Ciaglinski. That's the problem. There's no other problem, and that's why I'm unable to tell you who told me, "Ciaglinski was referring to you, wasn't he?" As I said, I didn't know the details until I came here. I asked for the session to be open, and I explained that the reason was everybody knew it was about me, so there was no reason for me to testify in closed session. That's why I agreed to an open session, and it was only then that I heard the details of what he said about me, that I was two metres tall, 180 kilogrammes in weight, an imposing figure, and so on and so forth. You all heard it. But neither my height nor my weight is as he described it, but that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the passage in the Milosevic trial that the witness is referring to where he has given what appears to be the same explanation, we would welcome that being identified by you and submitted in a filing to the -- to the Chamber as well, rather than us go through an appropriate material that is not before us. If you find the passage that you think records what he said on these terms, then we would welcome seeing that. Now, Mr. Kotur, please be clear in your mind that what the Prosecutor wanted was the names of one of the five or six people you say were present in the office when specifically your being mentioned in the trial was discussed; and I'm finding it difficult, I for one, why you won't tell us the name of even one of these people.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, gentlemen, Mr. Bonomy, if I said it was Colonel Ceda Nikolic or Ljubomir Pesic or Krsman Jelic or another of the colleagues that was there, I really don't know which one of them said, "Kotur, that was about you in closed session." And I said, "Yeah, I know that too." And somebody could go to that person and ask him, "Did you say that?" And -- well, a lot of people don't want to have any dealings with the Tribunal at all or with courts for no special reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, I've made it clear several times that the question is simply designed to get the identity of someone who was there, not the person who said it, because you've told us you can't remember that, but what I'm having difficulty understanding is why you won't even assist the Prosecutor with the inquiry to find out who it was who could support your account of this. In any event, that -- that matter is behind us now. These are the matters that -- these are the matters that I wished to raise with you. Now, Mr. Fila, what is it that you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecutor mentioned Sainovic once, and I want to put one question to him. Had he mentioned him twice, I would have put two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no logic to that approach. Tell me what the question is that you wish to put. It may be that it's to be put through the Court in this instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The question, Your Honour, is the following: When questioned about the conversation between Colonel Djakovic and Witness Kotur, when Colonel Djakovic talked about the meeting he had attended with Perisic and how the name "Joint Command" came into existence, later on it was mentioned that Sainovic and Andjelkovic arrived in Kosovo as civilians -- I mean Djakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've got Djakovic but into the meeting Perisic surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pavkovic. Yes, yes Pavkovic. I apologise. My only question that I wanted to put was the following: When did these civilians turn up? How long did they stay there in relation to the time when Colonel Djakovic told him he had attended that meeting in order to establish whether the arrival of Sainovic and Djakovic had anything to do with the meeting, and that would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Fila. Further cross-examination by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kotur, you mentioned a conversation between Colonel Djakovic and yourself and how the name "Joint Command" came into being. Then in response to a question from the Prosecutor, you said that at one point politicians arrived in Kosovo and you mentioned Sainovic and Andjelkovic. The question I want to put to you is the following: In relation to the conversation between you and Djakovic, the only one there was in June --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said June or July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in relation to that conversation, when did these politicians turn up? How long did they stay in Kosovo and -- well, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Andjelkovic turned up in the role of president of the temporary Executive Council, and my wife worked in his cabinet. The other gentlemen arrived from time to time to visit Andjelkovic in the Executive Council, and so I got this information from my wife. They would arrive to get information on the situation in Kosovo and Metohija and the terrorist groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But my question was when did they start arriving and until when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in August or September, in August and September, and they went to have a talk about that abduction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel and witness refrain from overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, what you said your wife told you and that --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic came later as president of the federal commission for relations with the verification mission. He was the president of that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When Colonel Djakovic told you that he had gone with General Pavkovic to attend a meeting at the MUP in June or July as you said, 1998, did he tell you who was there at that meeting, who attended it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I didn't object to Mr. Fila asking the one question he was going to ask on the 4th and it's something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We feel yet again that this is something that if you thought it important ought to have been dealt with much earlier in the examination. We all knew that the relationship between Djakovic and Pavkovic would be of significance and -- anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. Bakrac said he would use the transcripts, and he didn't use them; and the Prosecutor didn't say he would use them, but he did. How can I foresee who is going to ask what? I do apologise. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you have a specific question about Mr. Sainovic, then please ask it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did. I did, and that was all I wanted to ask. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you wanting to ask another one. That --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I don't want to ask anything else. I don't know why the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Life is full of surprises.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood the question to be whether there were any civilians at that coordination. If that's what he meant I don't have any such information that civilians attended the coordination meeting, Pavkovic -- meetings Pavkovic held in the MUP if that's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I have several questions to clarify certain points, and first let's start from what is freshest in our memory, the last few questions put by my learned friend. For how long did you know Mr. Ciaglinski?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Mr. Ciaglinski when he arrived in Kosovo and Metohija. I think on the 5th of December, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Apart from your official contacts did you have any other contacts with him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no other contacts with him apart from official ones while he was in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And when you had these official contacts with him, how did you communicate, because I understood you to say you didn't speak English.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We communicated through an interpreter, and there was always somebody there taking minutes, and very often that person would also speak English because they were from the Mip point, the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did the members of the Verification Commission use Albanians as interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not when they came to see us, but they did when they went elsewhere. However, according to our agreement, when he came to my office he didn't use Albanian interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, who were their interpreters then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had Serbs when communicating with us and Albanians when communicating with Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, you knew Ciaglinski from the 5th of December for about two months only officially and you communicated through interpreters. I have a very simple question. If you met someone only two months ago and if you communicate with someone only through interpreters, are you the kind of man who would be so open and disclose such a plan? Is that how you normally behave?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That's -- that calls for speculation, and it's -- I don't know what else, but it strikes me as improper and not helpful to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not asking him to speculate. I'm just asking him whether he is a man so open that after having known someone for only two months he would disclose to that person a plan of that kind. It's not speculation. I'm asking him if he's that sort of man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a leading question, Mr. Bakrac. It's quite inappropriate at this stage in the proceedings, so we'll move on to something else. Before we do, I would like CLSS to provide a translation of the tape from page 43, 19 to 23. The transcript doesn't record what was actually said in English and it would be interesting to see a proper translation -- a full translation, rather, of the B/C/S answer. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'll put my question in a different way. I'll rephrase it. What did Mr. Ciaglinski know about him and what did you know about Mr. Ciaglinski? Just be brief and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ciaglinski only knew my first and last name and that I was an infantry officer, that I had a wife and child, because he knew my wife since she worked in the Executive Council; and that's where we had offices and held our meetings. I knew about him, that he was an English intelligence officer, that he had worked in Germany, that he had a wife there, that he didn't have any children, that after the mission in Kosovo and Metohija he was going to be a military attache in Bulgaria, that he had served in Poland before that and that he was Polish by origin and had served in England. And I won't go on to list what else I knew about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, let's take a look at an exhibit now. It's also from near the end of Mr. Hannis's cross-examination. He showed you the minutes of ever a collegium. It's 3D1033. It's from December, and the question was whether Mr. Dimitrijevic had some information, whether he thought he had been misinformed --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: -- concerning the events in Podujevo in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 2 -- or, rather, the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This is an intelligence report. It appears to be dated the 19th, of the security organ of the Pristina Corps dated 19th December. Please -- you don't need to go back to page 1. It was sent to the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, and it was signed by chief Lieutenant-Colonel Momir Stojanovic. Do you know who that person was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know who Momir Stojanovic was. He was chief of the security organ of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was he subordinate to General Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you please read 3.1, the last paragraph.
